newsitem.title: USA: Comcast brings cable modem to more areas.
newsitem.headline: Comcast brings cable modem to more areas.

text.p: Comcast Corp said it was making high-speed Internet connections through cable modems available in three more of its major markets this week.

The company launched the service Tuesday in portions of its subscriber areas in the Philadelphia region and in Orange County, California, and will begin offering the service to portions of suburban Detroit on Thursday.
That will make the service available in at least parts of six of Comcast's top 10 markets, company officials said.

The service, called Comcast@Home, allows computer users to connect to the Internet through a high-speed modem attached to Comcast's coaxial television cable. It connects users to a home-area grouping of World Wide Web content into local and national sections of interest.
The service currently operates at about 1 million to 2 million characters per second, compared with about 33,000 characters per second through common modems using dial-up telephone lines.
That enables much quicker downloading of images, video clips and other information than ordinary home systems.

Jim Maguire, general manager of Comcast's Comcast Online division, told Reuters the system is technically capable of handling transmission speeds of 10 million characters per second, although that exceeds the capacity of many personal computers.
The system uses a proprietary "pipeline" developed by privately held @Home Network to deliver data at high speeds to regional centers near local service areas.
It also employs local "head-end" server computers to build storehouses of popular Internet sites and hasten user access.

@Home Network is owned jointly by Comcast, Cox Communications Inc and investor group Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers -- with a 14 percent interest each -- and Tele-Communications Inc, which owns 45 percent. The cable service providers together reach about 40 percent of U.S. homes.
Microsoft Corp on June 9 announced a $1 billion investment in Comcast aimed at hastening the convergence of computers with cable television.

The investment will help Comcast speed the upgrading of its system to handle the two-way traffic of Internet connections. The cable-modem system is being phased in as the network in each service area is upgraded.

Maguire said customer response to the service has been "rather brisk" in Baltimore, and Sarasota, Florida, where it was launched in December and January. "We're installing somewhere between 10 to 25 customers a day in each of our service areas, and that demand is getting greater," he said.
The service was also launched in northern New Jersey.
Nationwide, Comcast has about four million cable television subscribers.

Existing Comcast customers will pay $39.95 per month to for the service, which includes a cable modem and unlimited access. That compares with $19.95 per month for a commercial on-line service such as America Online Inc.
But Maguire said users of the Comcast service would not have to pay for an extra phone line also used by many dial-up Internet users, making the Comcast's price broadly competitive.
The cable modem, when in use, does not interfere with ordinary cable television service.

The Comcast service currently uses a customized browser by Netscape Communications Corp. Maguire said he expected Comcast to also offer a Microsoft Internet Explorer browser for the service in the future.
